questions.question: How has the undertaking conducted its double materiality assessment, and which sustainability matters were identified as material from both an impact and a financial perspective?

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Aker BP conducted its first double materiality assessment (DMA) in 2023 based on the CSRD and ESRS, and revised it in 2024 incorporating new implementation guidance and EFRAG's draft oil and gas sector standard. The assessment followed a four-step iterative process: (1) defining the business context including activities, business model, value chain, stakeholders and boundaries; (2) systematic identification of actual and potential IROs using top-down and bottom-up approaches with stakeholder input; (3) assessment and prioritization of IROs based on impact materiality (severity × likelihood) and financial materiality criteria using company risk scales; and (4) validation by management and the Board, with formal reporting and ongoing monitoring. Stakeholder engagement included in-depth interviews and workshops with owners, key suppliers, customers, NGOs and authorities. Impact materiality covers inside-out effects on environment and society, while financial materiality covers outside-in risks and opportunities including reputational risk and dependencies on natural, human and social resources. The material topics identified as strategic and highest priority (high on both impact and financial materiality) are: climate change, own workforce, pollution, business conduct, and resource use and circular economy. Additional material topics with significant impact but comparatively lower financial materiality include: affected communities, biodiversity and ecosystems, and workers in the value chain. Water and marine resources were assessed as having lower overall materiality but were added in 2024 as potentially material in the upstream value chain due to increased construction activity abroad. Cyber security was added as an entity-specific IRO under Governance. S4 Consumers and End Users was not identified as material. All material IROs were reviewed by the Board of Directors, Audit and Risk Committee, and Executive Management Team.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: BASF carried out a double materiality assessment in accordance with the ESRS for the first time in 2024, building on previous materiality assessments but with increased granularity and more extensive documentation. The assessment was performed at BASF Group level along the value chain in three steps: (1) compilation of a list of potential sustainability matters considering business impacts, customer industries, and stakeholder interests, using direct input from Advisory Councils, the BASF Civil Society Forum, multistakeholder networks, and indirect input from big data analyses; (2) identification and validation of risks and opportunities associated with the company's impacts and dependencies, working with in-house experts and selected stakeholders from the Nature Advisory Council and Human Rights Advisory Council, focusing on activities and value chain steps with elevated potential for negative impacts; (3) scoring of impacts, risks and opportunities on a 5-point scale using predetermined criteria (severity, scale, scope, and irremediability for negative impacts, plus likelihood of occurrence), classifying them as material when exceeding defined thresholds with higher weighting for negative impacts. The assessment was reviewed by interdisciplinary experts and the Board of Executive Directors, Supervisory Board, Joint Works Council and BASF Works Council Europe were informed. Material topics identified include: climate change (energy requirements), other environmental matters (emissions to air, water, and biodiversity), and the company's workforce as the main impact areas. ESRS S4 Consumers and End Users was assessed as not material given BASF's B2B business model. No entity-specific topics beyond those defined in the ESRS were identified. The results were further assessed for 'materiality of information' at the disclosure requirement and data point level using EFRAG criteria of 'decision-usefulness' and 'stakeholder relevance'.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Eni updated its 2024 materiality assessment based on ESRS standards to incorporate both perspectives of double materiality: impact materiality (inside-out) identifying significant positive and negative impacts on the environment and people, and financial materiality (outside-in) identifying risks and opportunities that may significantly affect the company's development, performance and financial position. The process included multiple phases: (1) identification of potentially relevant material topics using a top-down approach considering company objectives, benchmark analyses, ESRS and GRI industry standards, human rights due diligence results, and prior year assessments, incorporating stakeholder interests; (2) identification of IROs associated with potentially relevant topics, with impacts identified through public sources and internal managers, risks through the Integrated Risk Assessment process, and opportunities aligned with the Strategic Plan; (3) definition of the IRO assessment model with 1-to-5 scales for likelihood, significance (impact) and magnitude of effects (financial), using EFRAG guidelines; (4) assessment of IRO significance with impact materiality assessed through an IT platform by competent corporate functions and key subsidiaries, using a two-dimensional matrix with materiality thresholds (Tier 1 and 2 out of 3), and financial materiality aligned with the Integrated Risk Management model where Top Risks (Tier 1 and 2) are considered material; (5) engagement with targeted external experts on impact materiality results; (6) final calibration and prioritization, with results presented to the Control and Risk Committee, Sustainability and Scenarios Committee, Board of Statutory Auditors, and Board of Directors. Material topics from impact materiality include: climate change, pollution, water resources, biodiversity, resource use and circular economy, own workforce, workers in the value chain, affected communities, clients and consumers, business conduct, and innovation and cyber security. Financial materiality identified risks including climate change (physical and transition), accidents and blowouts, global security, biological risk, stakeholder relationships, and cyber security, along with multiple opportunities in energy transition, remediation, human resources, and supply chain sustainability.

evidence.text: The 2024 materiality assessment, aimed to identify the sustainability issues most relevant to Eni and its stakeholders, has been updated based on ESRS standards to include the two perspectives of double materiality, through: (i) the identification of the most significant impacts - positive and negative, actual and potential - generated by the organization on the environment and people, including human rights impacts (so-called 'impact materiality' or 'inside-out' perspective); (ii) the identification of risks and opportunities arising from sustainability related topics that may significantly affect the company's development, performance and financial position in the short, medium or long-term (so-called 'financial materiality' or 'outside-in' perspective).

evidence.text: For the impact materiality, the assessment was carried out by the competent corporate functions at central level through an IT platform that tracks the assessment process. A number of key subsidiaries were then involved to identify and assess potential additional impacts specific to their business/sector. On the basis of the overall assessments, impacts were selected as materials when, on the basis of a two-dimensional matrix that considers likelihood and relevance, they exceeded the materiality threshold defined internally (corresponding to Tier 1 and 2 out of a total of 3). For financial materiality, risks are assessed in terms of likelihood and magnitude of effects and represented in a matrix that distinguishes three areas (Tier 1, 2, 3 in descending order of importance): the risks in Tier 1 and Tier 2 categories are considered as the main risks of Eni or Top Risk.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Equinor conducted a comprehensive double materiality assessment (DMA) in 2024, building on its first DMA from 2023, following a structured four-step process aligned with ESRS and published implementation guidance. Step 1 established the business context by reviewing principal activities, business relationships, stakeholders, and dependence on key resources. Step 2 identified and assessed material IROs using the ESRS topic list, industry-specific lists from Ipieca and GRI, and Equinor-specific topics, drawing on operating data, internal/external studies, and stakeholder views. Impact materiality was assessed using severity criteria (scale, scope, remediability) with severity taking precedence over likelihood; both qualitative and quantitative thresholds were developed. Financial materiality was assessed using enterprise risk management framework thresholds measuring potential magnitude of financial effects and likelihood of occurrence. Step 3 validated results through internal calibration across management committees and external stress-testing with stakeholders. Step 4 implemented findings in the annual report. Material topics identified include GHG emissions, methane emissions, pollution, biodiversity impacts, human rights (from impact perspective), and climate change and energy transition risks and opportunities (from financial perspective). The DMA was formally anchored with the corporate executive committee, board audit committee, and board safety, sustainability and ethics committee.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Galp conducted its first Double Materiality Assessment in 2024, aligned with the EU CSRD, to identify and prioritise sustainability topics most critical to its business, affected stakeholders, and the environment. The assessment followed a six-step process: (1) identification of potential material topics through desktop review and peer benchmarking; (2) identification of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs); (3) definition of assessment criteria and scales based on EFRAG guidelines; (4) assessment of impact materiality evaluating actual and potential positive/negative impacts across the value chain; (5) assessment of financial materiality evaluating risks and opportunities affecting the company's development and performance; and (6) identification of material topics using varying stakeholder weights. The process was guided by ESRS and Double Materiality Implementation Guidance from EFRAG, and leveraged TCFD and TNFD frameworks. A bottom-up approach was used, first assessing materiality at business and geographic levels, then consolidating for the Galp Group. Results were approved by the Executive Committee and shared with the Sustainability Committee. Material topics identified from both impact and financial perspectives include: Climate change, Pollution, Biodiversity and Ecosystems, Water and Marine Resources, Health and Safety, and Human Rights.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: HELLENIQ ENERGY conducted a comprehensive Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) of sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities across its entire value chain for fiscal year 2024 and forward-looking periods (short-term 2025, medium-term 2026-2029, long-term 2030-2035). The DMA evaluated both impact materiality (how the Group's activities affect people and the environment) and financial materiality (how sustainability issues affect the Group's financial performance and value creation). The assessment followed a structured methodology involving stakeholder engagement, value chain mapping, IRO inventory development, and scoring against defined thresholds (Magnitude ≥4 and Likelihood ≥3 on 1-5 scales). The Group has been systematically implementing the impact assessment process since 2013. The assessment identified 16 material IROs across 6 material sustainability areas: (1) climate change mitigation and adaptation, (2) pollution of atmosphere, (3) health, safety and well-being, (4) economic impact, (5) mobility, and (6) energy (access and availability). Results were validated by Management and the Sustainability Committee of the Board of Directors.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: MOL Group introduced a new Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) methodology in 2024 to comply with CSRD requirements, following EFRAG's Materiality Assessment Implementation Guidance. The approach shifted from assessing the importance of sustainability topics to identifying material impacts on people and the environment, and financial risks and opportunities related to sustainability matters. The methodology involved three components: (1) Impact identification through stakeholder engagement with 75+ respondents, due diligence analyses, peer and sector studies, and deep-dive workshops with internal subject matter experts; (2) Risk identification using the Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) bottom-up process with Risk Owners and Risk Sponsors; (3) Opportunity identification aligned with the Shape Tomorrow Strategy. Impacts were rated by severity, risks were scored using the ERM methodology with USD 20-50M thresholds, and opportunities were aligned with strategic priorities. The assessment identified 22 material impacts (10 positive, 12 negative), 9 risks, and 11 opportunities. Material topics span environmental (climate change, pollution, biodiversity, resource use), social (own workforce, value chain workers, affected communities), and governance dimensions. The Sustainable Development Committee approved the DMA, while the Financial Risk Committee monitors financial and operational risks.

The Sustainability Committee (composed of Board members) approved the methodology and results, while the Sustainability Division conducted initial scoring with internal experts from relevant business units.

Material topics identified include: Climate Change (positive and negative impacts, regulatory risks, innovation opportunities), Pollution (regulatory compliance risks), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (waste utilization opportunities, ecosystem damage risks), Resource Use and Circularity (price volatility risks, material availability opportunities), Own Workforce (health and safety impacts and risks), Workers in the Value Chain (forced labor risks), and Business Conduct (positive impacts through ethical practices). A sustainability matter is material from an impact perspective when it pertains to Neste's material actual or potential, positive or negative impacts in relation to environmental, social and governance matters over short-, medium-, or long-term.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: OMV conducted its first materiality assessment under the ESRS framework in 2023, reviewed in 2024, applying the double materiality principle to evaluate both impact and financial materiality. The assessment was performed at Group level in five steps: (1) development of a long list of topics from ESRS, GRI, and SASB standards; (2) expert interviews to identify impacts, risks, and opportunities; (3) consultation with ten internal and external stakeholder groups (employees, customers, suppliers, capital market participants, NGOs, authorities, communities, associations, media, and research organizations); (4) assessment and scoring by subject matter experts in workshops to determine impact and financial materiality; (5) prioritization by defining thresholds. For impact materiality, a threshold of 8 was used for environmental topics (per EFRAG recommendations) and 5 for social and governance aspects. The financial materiality threshold was defined at 1.5, covering high and upper-range medium financial effects. Nine out of ten ESRS sustainability topics were identified as material (excluding climate adaptation and corruption/bribery at corporate level). Entity-specific topics such as process safety, cybersecurity, and economic impact were also identified as material.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Repsol conducted its double materiality assessment pursuant to CSRD through a structured five-phase methodology: (1) Analysis of context and business model across all geographies and the extended value chain (Exploration and Production, Industrial, Customer, Low Carbon Generation); (2) Stakeholder map and consultation identifying 9 groups and 40 subgroups, with over 550 responses gathered through questionnaires, interviews, and working groups; (3) Identification of topics, subtopics, and potentially material IROs with traceability to ESRS standards; (4) Evaluation of IROs by expert areas and stakeholders using CSRD-specified variables (for impacts: extent, irremediability, probability, magnitude on 1-5 scales; for risks/opportunities: potential financial effects and probability); (5) Results validation with combined thresholds. The assessment identified 44 material impacts and 17 risks and opportunities. Material topics from impact perspective include climate change (energy transition, decarbonization, renewable/non-renewable energy), pollution (air, water, soil), biodiversity, resource use and circular economy, talent management, health and safety, workers in value chain, community relationships, and customer satisfaction. Financial risks include transition regulatory changes, climate litigation, and raw material shortages, with opportunities in new low-carbon markets and products.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: SBM Offshore conducted its 2023 double materiality assessment through a structured 6-step process to evaluate both impact and financial materiality. The process involved: (1) Stakeholder mapping and long-listing of topics using industry benchmarks and standards; (2) Defining impact materiality through internal and external stakeholder engagement via questionnaire evaluating scope, scale, irremediability and likelihood; (3) Defining financial materiality with strategy, risk, finance and sustainability professionals analyzing how topics generate financial effects; (4) Applying a materiality threshold to cross-referenced impact and financial scores; (5) Validating with key internal and external stakeholders and senior management; (6) Updating in 2024 to align with ESRS, resulting in six final material topics: Emissions, Decommissioning, Our People, Health/Safety/Security, Human Rights, and Ethics/Compliance. Six additional topics were classified as purely business and strategic but not material per ESRS (Market position, Economic impact, Energy Transition, Operational Excellence and Quality, Innovation and Digitalization). per_company.ground_truth_answer: Shell conducted its double materiality assessment following a five-step process. Step 1 established the business context by reviewing principal activities, business relationships, and stakeholder groups while considering dependence on key resources (financial capital, operations, human capital, relationships, intellectual capital, natural resources). Step 2 identified impacts, risks and opportunities by reviewing ESRS topics, industry-specific lists from Ipieca and GRI, and Shell-specific topics. Step 3 assessed impacts for actual and potential severity using a five-point scale based on likelihood and magnitude. Step 4 reviewed potential financial effects using Shell's enterprise risk management framework with a five-point scale. Step 5 applied thresholds to determine material disclosures, with reporting requirements having at least one corresponding impact, risk or opportunity deemed material. The assessment identified GHG emissions as a material impact from both impact and financial perspectives, with climate change and energy transition identified as material sustainability-related risks and opportunities. A consolidated list of IROs is reviewed with internal experts and managers, with thresholds based on magnitude for actual impacts and combination of likelihood and magnitude for potential impacts.

Impact materiality was assessed using severity and likelihood scores with a threshold of 8, while financial materiality used magnitude and likelihood with a threshold of 3. Material topics identified span environmental (climate change, energy, pollution, water consumption, land-use change, biodiversity and ecosystems, waste), social (own workforce health and safety, workers in value chain, working conditions, diversity), and governance (business integrity, corruption prevention, whistleblower protection) dimensions. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Vopak conducted a Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) in 2024, aligning with ESRS 1 General Requirements, building on a GRI-aligned materiality assessment performed in 2022 and expanded in 2023 to encompass both impact and financial materiality. The process followed a structured three-phase approach for impact materiality: (1) Define impacts by reviewing previously reported topics against updated regulatory, sectoral, and voluntary reporting requirements (CDP, SASB, DJSI, GRI), refining topic definitions, and conducting stakeholder mapping; (2) Assess impacts with stakeholders through an online survey distributed to a broad stakeholder group for structured feedback on impact materiality; (3) Analysis and results with stakeholder feedback anonymized and analyzed independently. For financial materiality, an internal assessment was conducted with Internal Audit (for risks) and business development, financial analysis, global operations, and the Strategic Committee (for opportunities), scoring based on likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of potential financial effects. The highest score (risk or opportunity) was plotted on the materiality matrix to avoid underestimation. Results were validated by the Executive Board, which defined thresholds categorizing topics into three levels: essential (threshold ≥3), relevant, and enabler. Six essential topics were identified: GHG reduction and climate change mitigation (E1), Emissions to air/pollution (E2), Occupational health and safety (S1), Process safety and prevention of spills (S1), Workers in the value chain (S2), and Business ethics and integrity (G1). Topical standards E3, E4, E5, S3, and S4 were assessed as not applicable.

evidence.text: In preparation for the EU CSRD, Vopak conducted a Double Materiality Assessment (DMA) in 2024, aligning with ESRS 1 General Requirements. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Aker BP integrates sustainability-related performance into its incentive schemes through its company-wide bonus programme, which applies to all permanent employees including management. Approximately 22 percent of the bonus potential is dependent on sustainability-related initiatives and targets. The bonus scheme is defined as variable remuneration and utilises seven of eight equally weighted KPIs, along with initiative achievements and delivery on time, cost and quality through execution of key field development projects, as a basis. The eight KPIs are: Safety, Net production from operated assets, Adjusted production cost, Net reserve additions, Value creation, Relative shareholder return, Equity share scope 1 GHG intensity (kg CO2e/boe), and People and organisation. Notably, the KPI for people and organisation is solely based on employee feedback and does not factor into the bonus; only the remaining seven KPIs feed into the bonus calculation. The sustainability-related KPI in the bonus is equity share scope 1 GHG intensity (kg CO2e/boe). The organisational development and compensation committee (ODCC) is responsible for ensuring that remuneration arrangements support the company's strategy, including sustainability matters. The ODCC oversees the setting of targets and monitoring of progress related to KPIs linked to the incentive schemes for Executive Management Team (EMT) remuneration. The bonus is calculated with the same share of bonus potential for all employees. Supervisory Board (BoD) remuneration details are referred to the separate remuneration report.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: BASF integrates sustainability-related performance into its incentive schemes through both long-term and short-term incentive programmes. In the long-term incentive (LTI) for the Board of Executive Directors and senior executives, reducing Group-wide CO2 emissions (Scope 1 and Scope 2) is one of three equally weighted strategic targets (33.3% weight each), anchored since 2020. The Supervisory Board remuneration does not include any variable components and is therefore not linked to target achievement. In 2024, BASF introduced a short-term incentive (STI) programme for senior executives in operating business units, which includes, beyond financial targets, three additional targets: occupational and process safety, sustainability, and development of the operating divisions. The first two targets (occupational/process safety and sustainability) are sustainability-related. These three non-financial objectives are equally weighted in the STI calculation and together account for 25% of the total STI formula, meaning 16.7% of the entire STI formula is sustainability-related. The sustainability target in the STI includes elements contributing to the green transformation, such as sales of Sustainable-Future Solutions and increasing the share of purchased raw materials with supplier-specific Product Carbon Footprints.

evidence.text: We anchored reducing our Group-wide CO2 emissions (Scope 1 and Scope 2) as the most important nonfinancial key performance indicator in the BASF Group's steering and compensation systems back in 2020, giving it even more weight. This is one of three equally weighted (33.3%) strategic targets for the long-term incentive (LTI) of the Board of Executive Directors and senior executives. Supervisory Board remuneration does not include any variable components and so is not linked to target achievement.

In addition to the financial targets, this defines three further targets: occupational and process safety, sustainability and development of the operating divisions. The first two targets mentioned are sustainability-related. All three objectives are equally weighted in the STI calculation and together account for 25% of the total STI formula. This means that 16.7% of the entire STI formula is sustainability-related.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Galp integrates sustainability-related performance into incentive schemes for its administrative, management, and supervisory bodies through a performance evaluation framework anchored in ESG criteria directly linked to annual variable remuneration. Long-term incentives include Galp shares for the Executive Committee vested after four years, with attribution based partly on reduction of sales carbon intensity. per_company.ground_truth_answer: Repsol integrates sustainability-related performance into incentive schemes through a comprehensive multi-level framework. Achievement scales are defined for each metric with minimum compliance thresholds and maximum levels at 100%. The Remuneration Policy was approved by the General Shareholders' Meeting in May 2023. evidence.text: In the case of employees with annual variable remuneration, this remuneration is based on both the individual objectives of each employee and on the objectives of the business units. By 2024, objectives related to environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues have been integrated into all the objectives of each business unit, reaching a weight between 20% and 45%. In the particular case of the CEO, the weight of the objectives related to decarbonization and sustainability represents, in 2024, 25% of his annual variable remuneration.

evidence.text: In addition, Repsol has implemented a Long-Term Incentive (LTI) for the period 2024-2027, which affects all management staff, including the CEO, and other employees, in which 40% of the objectives are linked to the energy transition. questions.question: Does the undertaking have a transition plan for climate change mitigation? If yes, is the transition plan aligned with the objective of limiting global warming to 1.5°C? If no transition plan exists, what is the undertaking's timeline for adopting one?

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Aker BP does NOT have a transition plan for climate change mitigation as defined by the ESRS. The company explicitly states: 'Aker BP does not have any targets to reduce our scope 3 emissions. As a result, we do not have a climate transition plan in line with the ESRS' requirements and do not have a timeline for if or when we will develop such a plan.' While the company has set Scope 1 and 2 emission reduction targets (50% by 2030 and near zero by 2050 compared to 2017 baseline), these targets are described as 'not science-based' and not aligned with the 1.5°C objective. The company does have a decarbonisation plan with operational emissions reduction measures (electrification, energy efficiency, CCS readiness), but this does not constitute a full ESRS-compliant transition plan due to the absence of Scope 3 targets.

evidence.source_section_header: E1-1 – Transition plan for climate change mitigation
evidence.text: Aker BP does not have any targets to reduce our scope 3 emissions. As a result, we do not have a climate transition plan in line with the ESRS’ requirements and do not have a timeline for if or when we will develop such a plan.

evidence.source_section_header: 2.4 Targets
evidence.text: We aim to reduce our operational control scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 50 percent by 2030 compared with our 2017 baseline of 1.25 million t CO₂e. By 2050, we aim to achieve near-zero operational control and equity share scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions.

evidence.source_section_header: 2.4 Targets
evidence.text: Our climate-related targets are not science-based but are in line with national and international expectations for emission reductions in our industry.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Despite the absence of an ESRS-compliant transition plan, the disclosure quality is High because Aker BP transparently and comprehensively addresses both parts of the question: (1) it explicitly states it does NOT have a transition plan per ESRS requirements due to absence of Scope 3 targets, and (2) it clearly states its existing targets are not science-based. The candid acknowledgment of limitations, combined with detailed disclosure of existing Scope 1&2 measures and a 2017 baseline, constitutes thorough disclosure.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, BASF has a comprehensive transition plan for climate change mitigation that is explicitly aligned with the 1.5°C objective. BASF aims to reduce Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 25% by 2030 compared to 2018 and to achieve net zero emissions by 2050. The targets are aligned with the IEA Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE) scenario, which is compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5°C. BASF plans to invest approximately €300 million in Scope 1 emission reduction measures and approximately €250 million in renewable energy supply between 2025 and 2028. Key decarbonization levers include electrification of steam crackers using renewable energy, use of CO2-free hydrogen, development of new low-emission production processes (e.g., methane pyrolysis, e-crackers), expansion of renewable electricity procurement, and carbon capture and storage. BASF has validated its Scope 1 and 2 targets through the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) as consistent with the 1.5°C pathway.

evidence.text: We want to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from our production processes (Scope 1) and our energy purchases (Scope 2) by 25% by 2030 compared to the base year of 2018, and are aiming to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.
It is compatible with limiting global warming to 1.5℃ based on the emission reduction pathways described by the International Energy Agency (IEA) in its study entitled "Net Zero by 2050."

The transition plan is embedded in our financial planning and was approved by the Board of Executive Directors and the Supervisory Board. It is based on investments of around €300 million in Scope 1 measures and €250 million in renewable energies between 2025 and 2028.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: BASF provides comprehensive disclosure with explicit 1.5°C alignment through IEA NZE scenario and SBTi validation. The transition plan includes specific targets, financial commitments, decarbonization levers, and timeline. Both parts of the question are fully addressed.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Yes, Eni has a comprehensive transition plan called the 'Decarbonization Plan' that is aligned with the 1.5°C objective. The plan's pathway has been identified through actions from major international scenarios aimed at achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2050 to help keep the global temperature rise within 1.5°C by 2100, with reference to IPCC category C1 and IEA NZE scenarios. The structure of the pathway is described as 'substantially compatible with these scenarios.' The company targets Net Zero Carbon Footprint (Scope 1+2) for Upstream by 2030, for Eni overall by 2035, and Net Zero Lifecycle GHG emissions and Net Carbon Intensity (including Scope 3) by 2050. The plan includes investments in renewables, biorefining, carbon capture and storage, and energy efficiency.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: TotalEnergies provides robust disclosure with structured zero-tolerance compliance program, 380 Compliance Officers, two-tier risk mapping, 100% training coverage of exposed functions, formal due diligence procedures, and explicit confirmation of zero convictions and fines in 2024.

per_company.ground_truth_answer: Vopak has comprehensive systems for anti-corruption and anti-bribery prevention including an Anti-Bribery & Corruption (ABC) Policy consistent with the United Nations Convention against Corruption, Code of Conduct applying globally to all employees, contractors, suppliers and partners, mandatory anti-corruption training every other year (over 90% completion rate in 2024), Fraud Risk Management policy with annual bottom-up fraud risk assessments at Business Unit level, and a Speak Up platform with third-party software for confidential and anonymous reporting. In 2024, 37 Speak Up cases were reported with 11 investigated with solid evidence (4 integrity & behavior, 2 fraud, 5 cyber crime). Specifically for bribery & corruption: there were zero confirmed incidents in 2024 (compared to 10 in 2023), no fines were paid concerning bribery and corruption cases, and there have not been any convictions related to these cases.

evidence.source_section_header: Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
evidence.text: At Vopak, we are committed to conducting our business fairly, transparently, and with integrity, while applying the highest ethical and legal standards. We do not make, offer, or authorize bribes or conduct any other form of unethical business practice. Our rules and procedures related to anti-corruption or anti-bribery are set out in our Anti-Bribery & Corruption (ABC) Policy, which is accessible to our employees. This policy is consistent with the United Nations Convention against Corruption.

evidence.source_section_header: Prevention and detection of corruption and bribery
evidence.text: All employees complete mandatory training on anticorruption and anti-bribery every other year. Fraud alerts are regularly shared within the company to raise awareness and mitigate control weaknesses. Any alleged violation of our anti-corruption or anti-bribery rules and procedures can be reported through our Speak Up platform (as previously described) and is then investigated by an independent team.

evidence.source_section_header: Number of convictions and amount of fines
evidence.text: No fines were paid concerning the bribery and corruption cases. As far as we are aware, there have not been any convictions related to these cases.

per_company.fulfillment_rationale: Vopak provides comprehensive disclosure of anti-corruption systems (ABC Policy, Code of Conduct, mandatory training, Fraud Risk Management policy, Speak Up platform) and transparent incident data (zero bribery/corruption incidents in 2024, zero fines, zero convictions), with detailed breakdown of all Speak Up cases investigated.
